identified_problem: D2 rated AI-use declarations Weak on capability verification, GenAI exposure and authorship assurance. Compliance with transparency mechanisms was often not assessed or relied on unverified self-disclosure [S423], students under-declare because of fear, peer norms and low trust [S449], [S460], and 16 of 118 students claimed to have used a tool that no student had accessed [R45]. Declarations do not change the underlying task [R96], [D03], and logged AI use did not identify students with larger assignment-exam gaps [J6].
recommended_redesign: Set the permitted AI level for each task from its learning outcome, using a scale such as the AIAS [R10], and state it in plain words in every brief [S069].

Do not rely on student-completed declarations as evidence of how AI was used, because they can be invented [R45]. Where AI use matters to the grade, capture it in a university-managed workspace instead (see the monitoring framework) [R77], [R17].

Keep a short structured declaration for transparency about outside tools, and assess AI use through a published, outcome-weighted rubric criterion with a no-AI route to the same marks [R91], [R17], [R10].

Make honest disclosure within the permitted level carry no penalty, handle misuse through the integrity process rather than mark adjustments, and pair the work with an individual check [S460], [S416], [R80].
justification: Finding: in a computing course of over 750 students, groups submitted their three best prompts with justifications and each student had a 10-minute viva, and students in the same group with a well-written report sometimes received clearly different marks based on the viva [R80]. In a computing coursework of about 200 students, compliance with the permitted AI limits could not be checked [S028]. Outside computing, a use statement plus verification log and checkpoints was associated with higher report scores (d = 0.96), but this is reported in an abstract only [S140]. Interpretation: declarations can set expectations and record responsible use, but individual assurance has to come from the paired check.
implementation_considerations: Cohort size: full logs and reflections can be read in small cohorts [R72]; medium cohorts need rubrics and checklists [R15], [R91]. In large cohorts simple declarations scale [R80], [S115], but detailed log review becomes impractical [R16], so review a sample.

Staff time: a plain declaration costs little, but grading critique and logs adds marking time that has rarely been measured [S423], [S108]. R80 ran a 10-minute viva for each of over 750 students but did not report staff hours.

Policy and training: one faculty added standard permitted-use text to all syllabi within 4 months using champions and expert support [S069], yet only 42% of its students felt adequately informed [S069]. Staff AI literacy is a prerequisite [S331], [R27].

Equity: disclosure avoids AI detectors, which are reported to be biased against non-native English writers [R15], [R28]. Unequal access to paid tools [R20], [R10], stigma for multilingual writers [S482] and disadvantage for weaker writers in reflections [R45] still need to be addressed.
evidence_status_basis: R80 (computing = Y; quality 2/5; over 750 students) combined group prompt submission and individual GenAI reflections with a 10-minute individual viva and reported descriptive outcomes, including fewer mark-review requests. R14 (computing = Y; over 140 students in 37 teams) required per-interaction declarations and reviewed them qualitatively, and S028 (computing = Y; about 200 students) set an assistive-only AI rule but found no reliable way to check compliance. R15 (computing = Y; 88 students) required declared and evidenced AI use. Outside computing, S140 (quasi-experimental, n = 34 vs 33, abstract only) and S415 (AIAS pilot, where the fall in misconduct may reflect policy change) are the only comparative evaluations. No controlled computing study shows that declarations improve learning or integrity outcomes.
risks_and_limits: A declaration records what a student says they did and cannot establish authorship or understanding [S423], [R45]. Students may under-declare or fabricate declarations [S449], [R45], and critique tasks risk performative compliance, since 41% of students in one computing course agreed they completed GenAI tasks just to meet the requirement [R91]. Reported falls in misconduct after the AIAS may partly reflect harder-to-detect misuse [S415].
